findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request returns
findings.body: The goroutines in Create (line 51), Delete (110), Update (135) and DeleteCollection (163) derive their timeout context from the handler's `ctx`. That context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request finishes, and Create/Update/Delete return right after spawning the goroutine. The legacy call then runs with an already-cancelled or soon-cancelled context. SQL-backed legacy storage will usually fail with `context canceled`, so the 'safe measure' legacy write silently does not happen. Detach cancellation with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a fresh context carrying the needed values) before applying the 10s timeout. The unit tests use `context.Background()`, so they cannot catch this.

findings.title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy duration
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure came from Storage, so it should call `recordStorageDuration`. As written, unified-storage failures are counted under the legacy metric, and the storage error metric for create is never incremented. The same mistake is in Update at line 129.

findings.title: Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy duration
findings.body: On `d.Storage.Update` error the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Storage update errors are therefore attributed to the legacy backend and storage metrics undercount failures.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with the storage metric
findings.body: In the async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy latency and errors get mixed into the storage series, which already has an entry for this call, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection.

findings.title: Delete builds a contextual logger but stores the unenriched d.Log in the context
findings.body: `log` is created with name, kind and method, but `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the base logger. The downstream Storage and Legacy deletes therefore lose those values. Every other method uses `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. Line 106 has a related inconsistency: the success path passes `name` as the kind label to `recordStorageDuration`, while the error path and the legacy goroutine pass `options.Kind`. That produces a high-cardinality, inconsistent metric label.

findings.title: Legacy update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object written to storage
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped the storage result in `updateWrapper` so legacy received the exact object that was persisted. Now the raw `objInfo` is passed to `Legacy.Update` in a goroutine. For patch/apply requests, `UpdatedObject` is recomputed against the legacy store's own copy. That copy can differ from unified storage, including its resourceVersion, which risks conflicts or divergent data. The same `objInfo` is also used concurrently with the request handler after the function returns.

findings.title: Errors from async legacy writes are neither logged nor surfaced
findings.body: The old code logged legacy failures with the object context. In the new goroutines (Create 55-56, Update 139-140, Delete 112-113, DeleteCollection 165-166) the error is only turned into a boolean for a metric and then discarded. When legacy diverges from unified storage there is no log line saying which object or why, which makes the 'safe measure' write effectively unobservable. Log the error with the name/kind logger in each goroutine.

findings.title: Tests never verify the async legacy write, which is the core of mode 3
findings.body: None of the Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests assert that the legacy store is called after a successful storage write (for example `assert.Eventually` plus `m.AssertCalled`). They also do not assert that it is not called when storage fails. The legacy goroutines run unsynchronized and may outlive the test. The mock is shared between the legacy and storage stores, so the 'legacy' mock setups are satisfied by whichever side calls first. All tests use `context.Background()`, so the request-context cancellation problem cannot be detected. The tests would pass even if the legacy write were removed.

findings.title: Unrelated go.work.sum churn including a duplicated entry
findings.body: The PR adds 16 unrelated checksum lines (azure sdk, otel, alertmanager and others). One of them, `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, duplicates the line directly above it. These look like accidental output from a local `go work sync` and add noise to a PR about dual-writer mode 3.
